name: ATD (1,4,6-androstatrienedione)

lead: ATD is a steroid-like supplement ingredient sold over the counter in the prohormone era, reportedly until around 2009. Muscle-building circles discuss it for limiting estrogen conversion, aiming for less water retention and fewer gynecomastia concerns.

It is described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor, binding the enzyme that makes estrogen from androgens and inactivating it. Support comes from enzyme studies and an old monkey study; no human trial of its effects on muscle, gynecomastia or appearance was found.

paras: It was sold as an oral supplement, usually alongside prohormones or steroids during a cycle. Products carried varied names.
No human safety data were found. It is banned in sport and can reportedly cause a positive boldenone test. Products under varied names can be hard to identify.

angle.text: ATD is a prohormone-era aromatase inhibitor used to limit conversion of androgens to estrogen, aiming for less water and fewer gynecomastia concerns. Lab data support the mechanism, and no human trial has tested the look-related claims.

lead: ATD (1,4,6-androstatriene-3,17-dione) is a steroid-type compound described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor: it binds the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into estrogens and permanently inactivates it in fat and other peripheral tissue [1][2]. People in muscle-building circles took it to hold down estrogen conversion, with the aim of keeping a drier, leaner look and avoiding estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia, which they associated with a better-looking physique [2][3].

It was sold over the counter in bodybuilding supplements, reportedly until 2009, in oral and topical forms and under many alternative names, and a T Nation poster describes it as a product still seen for sale and as a metabolite of boldenone [1][3]. Wikipedia credits supplement-industry figure Bruce Kneller with developing and commercialising it, and links the product to Gaspari Nutrition [1].

Published work consists of laboratory enzyme studies and an animal study; no human trial of ATD for body composition, gynecomastia or any other appearance outcome has been identified. It is prohibited in sports that ban aromatase inhibitors [1].
infobox: Oral; topical versions were also sold [1]
Former OTC supplement ingredient; banned in sport [1]

paras: ATD is described as binding aromatase and permanently inactivating it in fat and other peripheral tissue, which lowers estrogen production [1]. A 1981 study cited by Wikipedia described enzyme-generated intermediates that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [1]. A 1995 chemistry paper evaluated 4-thio-substituted derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione and related dienediones and reported potent inhibition of aromatase in human placental microsomes [4].

Aromatase inhibitors as a class are divided into irreversible steroidal types, such as exemestane, and reversible nonsteroidal types, such as anastrozole and letrozole [2]. Wikipedia lists reported effects of the class including reduced bone maturation, hair loss and liver dysfunction, and notes that they are used in men for hormone-sensitive cancers and sometimes off-label to manage estrogen during testosterone therapy [2]. These class effects were not measured for ATD itself.

ATD appeared in some over-the-counter supplements until 2009, and topical products were also marketed [1]. Wikipedia credits supplement-industry figure Bruce Kneller with developing and commercialising it and notes he holds a related US patent [1]. Sellers used many alternative names, which can make products harder to identify [1].

ATD is prohibited in amateur and professional sport as an aromatase inhibitor. It is also reported that ATD can produce a positive test for the anabolic steroid boldenone, of which it is a possible metabolite and manufacturing contaminant [1].
A 2009 paper cited by Wikipedia examined ATD metabolism and its detection by GC/MS in doping control [1]. ATD can be made from DHEA in a single oxidation step [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, a poster advising another lifter points to ATD (arimistane) as a suicidal aromatase inhibitor and a boldenone metabolite that could still be bought over the counter [3]. Searches of the forum for the abbreviation also return unrelated content, since the same letters name other things.

No studies found. A 1984 study in rhesus monkeys, cited by Wikipedia, reported that aromatase inhibition increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion; this was animal research and not a test of appearance outcomes [1].

lore.intro: ATD appears in muscle-building forums as an over-the-counter aromatase inhibitor, usually mentioned in passing in advice to other lifters [3].

claims.claim: ATD lowers estrogen so users stay lean and avoid gynecomastia
ATD is a legal over-the-counter option

timeline.event: Study describes enzyme-generated intermediates of ATD that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [1].
Rhesus monkey study reports raised LH and testosterone with aromatase inhibition [1].
Paper reports 4-thio derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione as potent aromatase inhibitors in vitro [4].
Approximate end of ATD's presence in over-the-counter supplements [1].
